<reason>Both sides argued competently, but CON built the more durable case. CON's central move—reframing "cost per contact" as the wrong unit versus "cost per resolution/liability/lost customer"—was introduced early, sharpened with a grounded real-world example (the Air Canada chatbot liability case), and never fully dislodged. PRO's attempt to flip that example into proof that "accountability exists" was clever but conceded the deeper point that liability and reputational cost are real and uncapped. More decisively, when PRO claimed in Rebuttal 2 that repeat-contact tracking already captures the "gave up" signal, CON's answer that permanently churned customers leave no trace in exactly those dashboards went unanswered in PRO's closing, which retreated to reasserting "structural certainty" rather than confronting the measurement-blindness charge. CON also handled the Pressure Questions exchange well, converting PRO's demand for hard numbers into a symmetry argument ("your savings claims lack numbers too") that PRO never fully overcame. PRO's case remained coherent and plausible throughout (cheap marginal cost, escalation design, "compared to what" framing), but it relied on asserting certainty it didn't actually demonstrate, and its opening being clipped for length is a real execution cost. CON's closing crystallized the clash more sharply than PRO's, leaving the decisive comparison unresolved in PRO's favor.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B4's answer to A4.1—arguing that a customer who simply never returns is invisible to the very repeat-contact metrics PRO relies on—directly undercut PRO's claimed solution to the "containment vs. resolution" problem and was never adequately answered in PRO's closing.</best_rebuttal>
